name: The Allen household — a name from the post office's letter lists

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RETURN, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The office's list of letters uncalled-for is a RETURN — its statement of what was still unclaimed on ONE day — and the paper reprinted one return over as many consecutive issues as it took, so the bound is dated by the return of June 1835 and not by the issue it was read in (T-0425). The earliest issue this project reads the name in is 1835-07-01, 1 day later; that gap is an accident of which impression an extraction pass reached, and it is not evidence. Somebody was writing to this name at Chicago by 1835-06-30 and at no stated time before it; nothing says when they came. The date lines the printings set, and how they were weighed, stand beside this rule in tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py.

arrival_year.note: DRAWN, NOT READ. The household's arrival block holds a BOUND — somebody was here by 1835-06-30 and no source says when they came — so the year is drawn from the arrival years the known layer records, truncated at that bound and renormalised. It says what a household of this bound most likely was, and nothing whatever about this household.

later_occupation.note: NONE RECORDED FOR 1835 — AND A TRADE IS RECORDED FOR 1839. This is a POINTER at `directories.people[].occupation_later` on this same record, derived by `tools/qualify_later_trades.py` and holding nothing that block does not already say. It is not a claim about the scene date: the 1835 occupation above still reads `none_recorded`, its grade has not moved, and no premises has been sought on the strength of it, because a directory of 1839 is evidence about 1839. It is written because the field a reader consults was asserting an absence this file contradicts three lines further down, and "no trade anywhere" and "no trade in the scene window, one printed 1839" are not the same fact (T-0693).

persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G2e, applied 2026-09-04. This identity is inferred because that rung fired on the civic and press rows recorded on this card, which the resident-research corpus does not read. This programme's letter-list rule of 2026-09-02 would call it a projected resident on the absence of a research row; it is superseded here, and a no-find in one corpus is not a finding about another (T-0822). KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Allen, William' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Wm. Allen” (33S7-9YYJ-NY, printed page 230, line 26). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (L6 matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (data/research/census_1840/resident_crosswalk.json). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Allen, Willard | Profession. | September 15, 1876.” (second_presb_0002, printed page 154), admitted 1876-09-15 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Allen' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins W. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('allen_william:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

sex_basis.note: A FORENAME THAT STANDS IN ONE SEX'S NAMING ONLY. 'William' is read as male because 4 persons in this layer whose sex a source records bear it (adams_william_h, egan_william_b, stow_william_h, walters_william), and it stands in the yankee male forename pool of this town's own attested naming. Nothing about this person is recorded; the name is the whole of the reasoning, and the table that licenses it — data/research/residents/forename_sex.json — refuses a name its own evidence splits, refuses Jean, Marion, Leslie and Francis by name, and refuses an initial outright.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.

surname_collision.refusal: the town already names a Allen
surname_collision.note: A COLLISION SAID, NOT ACTED ON. Run against the tree as it stands, this pass would not MINT this card: refusal 7 — 'the town already names a Allen' — lands on it, because Edward Richards Allen (hh_allen_edward_richards); Lieut. James Allen (hh_allen_lieut_james) already holds the family name Allen. The owner ruled on 2026-09-18 (T-0660, option (c)) that refusals 7 and 8 are MINT-TIME rules: they decide whether a new household may be minted on a family name the town already spends, and they do not un-mint one that already stands. So this record is not retired, its id is not redirected at anybody, the town's population does not move, and the research row and directory matches it carries are not stranded on a retirement nothing draws. What has changed is that the collision is legible: a reader sees both cards and why both are here. REFUSAL 7 IS NOT A CLAIM THAT TWO RECORDS ARE ONE PERSON — it is the precedence rule between this pass and the ones above it, which give a man the papers gave a trade the family name a letter list only spells. Two of the collisions this reading uncovered are two different men. The pass's `rank()` is unchanged and the cohort is not re-derived; that was option (b)'s cost and the ruling declined to pay it. The derivation behind this block, both readings side by side, is docs/RESEARCH/letter-list-surname-collisions.md.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. allen_william, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e0018 (a single entry); allen_william, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e0198 (a single entry); allen_william, Norris's Chicago directory of 1844 — n1844_e0019 (a single entry).

occupation_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this trade against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Allen, William, saloon, North Canal street south of Kinzie'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
